 Shapiro Wants a Minimum Wage Hike to Be the First Bill He Signs, but Democrats Haven’t Agreed on a Number
 ✓ 
 By 
 Angela Marchetti 
 Politics & Government Reporter 
 Published 
 November 6, 2026 
 3 min read 
 Share 
 𝕏 
 f 
 Make us a preferred source 
 Gov. Josh Shapiro says a minimum wage increase will be the “very first bill” he signs when his second term begins in January, the Philadelphia Inquirer reported. Democrats plan to move a minimum wage bill first now that they will control both chambers of the legislature, Spotlight PA reported.
 “We will raise the minimum wage,” Shapiro said Wednesday at a news conference outside the Governor’s Residence, according to Spotlight PA.
 Pennsylvania’s minimum wage is $7.25 an hour, the federal rate, and has not changed since 2009, the Inquirer and Spotlight PA reported.
 The $15 bill and the split over the number
 The state House passed H.B. 2189 in March, which would raise the wage in steps to $15 by 2029 and then tie it to inflation, the Inquirer reported. Earlier $15 bills also passed the Democratic House and died in the Republican-controlled Senate, according to the Inquirer.
 Democrats have not settled on a figure, Spotlight PA reported. Sen. Vincent Hughes (D., Philadelphia) wants to “double that sucker,” according to Spotlight PA, while Sen. Lisa Boscola (D., Northampton) told Spotlight PA, “If they talked about $20, I would say no.”
 “Half a million workers in Pennsylvania still make less than $15 an hour,” Shapiro wrote in a post on X on Wednesday, the Inquirer reported. The Inquirer, citing 2025 state Labor and Industry estimates, reported that about 42,900 Pennsylvania workers earned the minimum or less, about 189,900 earned $7.26 to $12 and about 320,900 earned $12.01 to $15.
 Rep. Matt Bradford (D., Montgomery) urged caution, telling reporters on Wednesday, “We have a mandate, yes. But it’s a mandate for what we talked about when we were at 102,” followed by “humility,” Spotlight PA reported.
 The business and Republican view
 When the House passed H.B. 2189 in March, Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman said any change should be a “commonsense adjustment” that takes small businesses and nonprofits into account, the Inquirer reported. The Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry warns that a higher wage could cost jobs and hours, according to the Inquirer.
 What it could mean in Philadelphia
 The MIT living wage calculator puts the cost of living for a single adult with no children in Philadelphia at about $25.38 an hour, the Inquirer reported. The union SEIU 32BJ wants state law changed so Philadelphia can set its own $20 minimum, according to the Inquirer.
 Mayor Cherelle L. Parker said in a statement on Election Day that “we don’t have an affordability crisis if what we earn gives us the ability to take care of ourselves,” the Inquirer reported.
 The minimum wage is one of several Philadelphia priorities riding on the new majority. The Inquirer reported that SEPTA projects a $192 million operating deficit next fiscal year, and Shapiro said Wednesday, “We will fund mass transit,” according to Metro Philadelphia. City Council President Kenyatta Johnson called the results “a historic opportunity” to line up the city, Harrisburg and Washington on schools, housing, transit and public safety, Metro Philadelphia reported.
 No bill has been introduced yet, and the new legislative session begins in January. Democrats said they would soon announce a “first 100 days” agenda, WITF and Metro Philadelphia reported.
